old: The people here cannot abide strangers, and do not like men who come from somewhere else.
new: The people here are wary of strangers at first, and do not much like men who come from somewhere else.
reason: Reads as a flat contradiction within this same chapter: moments later Alcinous and his household welcome Odysseus with extraordinary warmth, feed him, and offer their daughter's hand. A first-time listener has nothing to reconcile the two claims with.

old: Periboea was the youngest daughter of Eurymedon, who at one time reigned over the giants, but he ruined his ill-fated people and lost his own life as well.
new: Periboea was the youngest daughter of Eurymedon, king of the giants, whose recklessness destroyed his own people and cost him his life.
reason: The pronoun "he" and the string of unexplained names (Periboea, Eurymedon, the giants) pile up in one sentence with no anchor; a listener has to work to figure out who ruined whom.

old: But he left a daughter, Arete, whom Alcinous married
new: But Rhexenor left a daughter, Arete, whom his brother Alcinous later married
reason: "He" is ambiguous (could be misread as Nausithous or Alcinous rather than the just-mentioned Rhexenor), and the unstated fact that Alcinous married his own niece is likely to stop a first-time listener cold with no clarification offered.

old: where she entered the home of Erechtheus
new: where she entered the home of Erechtheus, the legendary king of Athens
reason: Erechtheus is named with no context; a general listener won't know who this is or why Athena's stop there matters.

old: the linen is so closely woven that it sheds oil
new: the linen is so tightly woven that oil beads and runs right off it
reason: Abrupt topic pivot mid-sentence (from the shuttle simile to a claim about the cloth) and an odd, under-explained image ("sheds oil") that a listener has to stop and puzzle over.

old: who takes all well-disposed suppliants under his protection
new: who watches over all who come here in good faith seeking help
reason: "Suppliants" is formal/archaic vocabulary a general listener may not recognize, and it recurs verbatim (see paragraph 15) without ever being explained.

old: who is the protector of all well-disposed suppliants
new: who protects all who come here in good faith seeking help
reason: Near-identical phrasing to paragraph 14's "suppliants" line repeated within a few lines; the repeated archaic term compounds the earlier flag rather than varying the language.

old: even if it is a long way further off than Euboea. When my people took yellow-haired Rhadamanthus to see Tityus the son of Gaia, those of them who saw it told me it is the furthest place of any.
new: even if it is a long way further off than Euboea, which my sailors once reached on a single day's voyage while ferrying a passenger there and back — by all accounts the furthest place anyone has sailed to.
reason: Four unexplained proper nouns (Euboea, Rhadamanthus, Tityus, Gaia) land in two sentences with no context for who these figures are or why the anecdote proves anything; a first-time listener is likely to lose the thread of Alcinous's boast entirely.
